clue.text: Exclusive property, often used in films

blocks.note: something exclusive is special, reserved for a few
personal effects are one's belongings or property

explanation.surface: An estate agent's description of a private house that film crews like to hire as a location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exclusive property' reads as one estate-agent phrase, but the two words are clued separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Explosions, monsters and other screen illusions created by technicians are a staple of cinema, so the phrase describes something movies frequently employ.

clue.text: Such a banner might produce rapt gladness

indicators.note: to produce something from raw material is to make it anew, so the letters are worked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A patriotic flag might stir up rapt joy in the people watching it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Star-Spangled Banner is the US flag and national anthem, which an American crowd might well greet with rapt gladness.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective completes the anthem's title, so a banner of this kind is the American flag strewn with stars.

clue.text: Headless nobleman? That's spooky!

indicators.note: without a head means the opening letter of the word is lopped off

blocks.note: a peer is a member of the nobility

explanation.surface: A beheaded aristocrat appears, and someone exclaims at how creepy it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' looks like part of the exclamation but stands for i.e., Latin for 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spooky and eerie are synonyms, both describing something strange and frightening in a ghostly way.

clue.text: One kid follows everyone around, making us uncomfortable

indicators.note: turning around makes the word face the other way, so it is read backwards

blocks.note: to kid someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: A child trails after the whole group, which makes them all feel awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child but is the verb meaning to tease; 'follows' puts it after the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ill at ease is to feel uneasy or awkward, the idiom for being uncomfortable.

clue.text: Free translation from Braille

indicators.note: a translation renders a text in a different form, so these letters are recast in a new order

explanation.surface: A loose rendering of a text out of the raised-dot alphabet for blind readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free translation' is a set phrase, but 'Free' is the definition and 'translation from' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal can mean loose or not literal, as in a liberal translation, and so is a synonym of free.

clue.text: Dissenters start to foment armed conflict

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: soldiers in action are in combat

explanation.surface: Rebels begin stirring up a war.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction is a dissenting group within a larger body, so the plural noun is matched by a collective noun.

clue.text: Guarantee shortage of runs will provide result

indicators.note: a shortage means something is missing, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: to guarantee is to make sure
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricket pundit promises that a lack of runs will decide the match.
explanation.walkthrough: The R for runs is removed from the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow as a consequence, so the verb is a synonym of result in the sense of happen afterwards.

clue.text: Couple caress gently, with an up-and-down movement

blocks.note: to stroke is to caress gently

explanation.surface: Two lovers tenderly fondle each other in a rhythmic motion.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is romantic, but the definition is mechanical: a two-stroke engine's piston rises and falls once per power cycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-stroke engine completes its cycle in one upward and one downward piston travel, so the adjective describes that reciprocating motion.

clue.text: A month in Capri? Lovely!

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the following words, running across them

explanation.surface: Someone imagines spending a month on the Italian island of Capri and sighs with delight.
explanation.definitionFit: April is the fourth month of the year, so it is an example of a month.

clue.text: Supports first-class baseball player

explanation.surface: Someone praises a superb baseball player for propping up the team.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball a backstop is the catcher, the player crouched behind home plate who stops the pitches.

clue.text: In person they represented threat to health

indicators.note: to be represented is to be shown in another form, so the letters are set out differently

explanation.surface: People appearing face to face posed a danger to public health, as in a pandemic.
explanation.definitionFit: High blood pressure raises the risk of strokes and heart disease, so it is a serious medical danger.

clue.text: You'll be one in one when it's hot

definitions.text: You'll be one in one when it's hot

blocks.clueFragment: You'll be one in one when it's hot
blocks.note: surface reading: a riddle about being some kind of thing inside the same kind of thing in warm weather
setter's reading: the first 'one' is a person who perspires, the second a woollen jumper, and the same word names both

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both someone perspiring and a knitted pullover, so wearing one on a hot day makes you one in one.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a knitted top and also, literally, a person who perspires heavily.

clue.text: In ecstasy Ruth lay oddly, without moving

indicators.note: oddly means taking the odd-numbered positions, first, third and so on

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Ruth lay in a blissful trance, strangely motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In ecstasy' reads as one phrase, but 'In' is literal letters and 'ecstasy' is the drug, abbreviated E.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means motionless or inactive, so the adverb describes doing something while staying perfectly still.

clue.text: Lost whilst sailing

blocks.note: second meaning: out on the ocean during a voyage

explanation.surface: A boat goes missing during a voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means bewildered, and literally it means out on the ocean, which is where a sailing ship is.

clue.text: Excitement about a container for apples and pears?

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a stir is a commotion or excitement

explanation.surface: A fuss is made over a box for holding fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apples and pears' is Cockney rhyming slang for stairs; the question mark flags that the fruit is not fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang apples and pears means stairs, and a staircase is a flight of stairs.

clue.text: Where to get tan or laze about

definitions.text: Where to get tan or laze about

indicators.note: about suggests moving things around, so the preceding letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A recommendation for a place to sunbathe and lounge around.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while the middle words supply its letters: Lanzarote is a sunny Spanish island in the Canaries, popular with British holidaymakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanzarote is a Canary Island resort known for beaches, a classic destination for sunbathing and relaxing.

clue.text: Skill with which I restrict growth of plant

blocks.note: art is skill, as in the art of persuasion
weeds choke plants by stunting their growth

explanation.surface: A gardener boasts of the technique used to stunt a plant's growth.
explanation.definitionFit: The artichoke is a thistle-like plant grown for its edible flower head, so it is an example of a plant.

clue.text: Sherpa got shoddy ammunition

indicators.note: shoddy means badly made, so the letters are put together in a poor, jumbled order

explanation.surface: A Himalayan mountain guide was supplied with poor-quality bullets.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapeshot is a cluster of small iron balls fired from a cannon, a historic type of munition.

clue.text: Pagan woman finally converted

indicators.note: converted at the end means the last letter is swapped for a different one

explanation.surface: A woman who once held pagan beliefs eventually changed her religion.
explanation.walkthrough: Changing the final R of the name to N gives the answer; the clue does not say which letter replaces it, so the definition must confirm it.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone who does not follow a major religion, an old synonym for pagan.

clue.text: Fictional native American tours Oregon city

indicators.note: to tour a place is to travel round it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: Tonto is the Lone Ranger's Native American companion
OR is the postal abbreviation for Oregon

explanation.surface: A storybook Native American character travels around a city in Oregon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oregon city' reads as one phrase, but Oregon is just the state abbreviation and 'city' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is the largest city in Canada and the capital of Ontario.

clue.text: The fort's gold is snatched in robbery

indicators.note: something snatched is taken away, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A fortress's bullion is seized in a raid.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft is the act of stealing, so it is a synonym of robbery.

clue.text: Recalling road south, a road in French landmass

indicators.note: recalling means calling back, so the string of pieces is read backwards

blocks.note: the A1, written AI, is the Great North Road in Britain
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Someone remembers roads in France while thinking about a continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, and crosswords write its 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasia is the combined continent of Europe and Asia, the largest continuous area of land on Earth.

clue.text: Hunks show off how to get large muscles

indicators.note: off means removed, so those letters are taken out of the word before it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Muscular men flaunt their physique, demonstrating how to bulk up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show off' looks like a phrasal verb about the hunks, but 'off' removes the next word from 'show', leaving a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunk is a large thick piece of something, as is a slab, so the plurals are synonyms.

clue.text: Animal managed to incubate 200 eggs

indicators.note: a bird incubates eggs by sitting over them, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
C is the Roman numeral for 100
an egg's shape resembles the letter O

explanation.surface: A creature somehow managed to brood two hundred eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: The raccoon is a ringtailed, masked North American mammal, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Shop also stocks gemstones

indicators.note: a shop that stocks goods keeps them inside, so the answer is held within the surrounding words

explanation.surface: A jeweller's store sells precious stones as well.
explanation.definitionFit: The opal is an iridescent silica mineral cut and polished for jewellery, so it is a kind of gem.

clue.text: Athletic event, almost more than a sport

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the word loses its last letter
sport here is a verb sense of play or frolic, so the letters romp into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone says a gruelling race is nearly something greater than a mere sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport' looks like a noun completing the phrase, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A marathon is a long-distance running race of about 26 miles, a classic track-and-field competition.

clue.text: Arab's returning soon

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way it went, so the phrase is read from end to start

explanation.surface: An Arab man will be back shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arab's' reads as possessive but is 'Arab is'; 'in a mo' is British slang for in a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: An Omani is a native of Oman, a country on the Arabian Peninsula, so an Omani is an Arab.

clue.text: Involving contact with Argentinian boy drinkers in prison

indicators.note: someone in prison is locked inside, so these pieces are enclosed by the surrounding name

blocks.note: Juan Perón was president of Argentina
a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: Someone has links with an Argentine lad whose drinking mates are behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In prison' reads as where the drinkers are, but it says the Argentinian surname, that of President Perón, locks the boy and drinkers inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Person-to-person describes direct dealings between individuals, communication that involves people meeting or speaking directly.
